entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 14 Zec 14:1-21 . Last Struggle with the Hostile World-Powers: Messiah-Jehovah Saves Jerusalem and Destroys the Foe, of Whom the Remnant Turns to the Lord Reigning at Jerusalem. 1. day of the Lord-- in which He shall vindicate His justice by punishing the wicked and then saving His elect people ( Joe 2:31 ; 3:14 ; Mal 4:1, 5). thy spoil ... divided in the midst of thee-- by the foe; secure of victory, they shall not divide the spoil taken from thee in their camp outside, but "in the midst" of the city itself.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13193"/><div sID="gen24904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13193"/><hi type="bold">2. gather all nations, &c.--</hi>The prophecy seems literal (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.2">Joe 3:2</reference>). If Antichrist be the leader of the nations, it seems inconsistent with the statement that he will at this time be sitting in the temple as God at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>); thus Antichrist outside would be made to besiege Antichrist within the city. But difficulties do not set aside revelations: the event will clear up seeming difficulties. Compare the complicated movements, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.1-Dan.11.45">Da 11:1-45</reference>.<div eID="gen24904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">half ... the residue--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>, it is "two-thirds" that perish, and "the third" escapes. There, however, it is "in all the land"; here it is "half of the city." Two-thirds of the "whole people" perish, one-third survives. One-half of the citizens are led captive, the residue are not cut off. Perhaps, too, we ought to translate, "a (not 'the') residue." <div eID="gen24905" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13195"/><div sID="gen24908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13195"/>4. The object of the cleaving of the mount in two by a fissure or valley (a prolongation of the valley of Jehoshaphat, and extending from Jerusalem on the west towards Jordan, eastward) is to open a way of escape to the besieged (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.12">Joe 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.14">14</reference>). Half the divided mount is thereby forced northward, half southward; the valley running between. The place of His departure at His ascension shall be the place of His return: and the "manner" of His return also shall be similar (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>). He shall probably "come from the east" (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.27">Mt 24:27</reference>). He so made His triumphal entry into the city from the Mount of Olives from the east (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.10">Mt 21:1-10</reference>). This was the scene of His agony: so it shall be the scene of His glory. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">Eze 11:23</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>, "from the way of the east." <div eID="gen24908" type="x-p"/>

Half the divided mount is thereby forced northward, half southward; the valley running between. He so made His triumphal entry into the city from the Mount of Olives from the east ( Mt 21:1-10 ). This was the scene of His agony: so it shall be the scene of His glory. Compare Eze 11:23 , with Eze 43:2 , "from the way of the east."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13196"/><div sID="gen24909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13196"/><hi type="bold">5. ye shall flee to the valley--</hi>rather "through the valley," as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.29">2Sa 2:29</reference>. The valley made by the cleaving asunder of the Mount of Olives (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zec 14:4</reference>) is designed to be their way of escape, not their place of refuge [Maurer]. Jerome is on the side of English Version. If it be translated so, it will mean, Ye shall flee "to" the valley, not to hide there, but as the passage through which an escape may be effected. The same divinely sent earthquake which swallows up the foe, opens out a way of escape to God's people. The earthquake in Uzziah's days is mentioned (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>) as a recognized epoch in Jewish history. Compare also <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Is 6:1</reference>: perhaps the same year that Jehovah held His heavenly court and gave commission to Isaiah for the Jews, an earthquake in the physical world, as often happens (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">Mt 24:7</reference>), marked momentous movements in the unseen spiritual world.<div eID="gen24909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the mountains--</hi>rather, "of My mountains," namely, Zion and Moriah, peculiarly sacred to Jehovah [Moore]. Or, the mountains formed by My cleaving Olivet into two [Maurer].<div eID="gen24910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Azal--</hi>the name of a place near a gate east of the city. The Hebrew means "adjoining" [Henderson]. Others give the meaning, "departed," "ceased." The valley reaches up to the city gates, so as to enable the fleeing citizens to betake themselves immediately to it on leaving the city.<div eID="gen24911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord my God ... with thee--</hi>The mention of the "Lord my God" leads the prophet to pass suddenly to a direct address to Jehovah. It is as if "lifting up his head" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">Lu 21:28</reference>), he suddenly sees in vision the Lord coming, and joyfully exclaims, "All the saints with Thee!" So <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">Is 25:9</reference>.<div eID="gen24912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saints--</hi>holy angels escorting the returning King (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">Mt 24:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">31</reference>; Jude 14); and redeemed men (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">1Co 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">1Th 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">4:14</reference>). Compare the similar mention of the "saints" and "angels" at His coming on Sinai (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.53">Ac 7:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.2">He 2:2</reference>). Phillips thinks Azal is Ascalon on the Mediterranean. An earthquake beneath Messiah's tread will divide Syria, making from Jerusalem to Azal a valley which will admit the ocean waters from the west to the Dead Sea. The waters will rush down the valley of Arabah, the old bed of the Jordan, clear away the sand-drift of four thousand years, and cause the commerce of Petra and Tyre to center in the holy city. The Dead Sea rising above its shores will overflow by the valley of Edom, completing the straits of Azal into the Red Sea. Thus will be formed the great pool of Jerusalem (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zec 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.18">Joe 3:18</reference>). Euphrates will be the north boundary, and the Red Sea the south. Twenty-five miles north and twenty-five miles south of Jerusalem will form one side of the fifty miles square of the Lord's Holy Oblation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:1-35</reference>). There are seven spaces of fifty miles each from Jerusalem northward to the Euphrates, and five spaces of fifty miles each southward to the Red Sea. Thus there are thirteen equal distances on the breadth of the future promised land, one for the oblation and twelve for the tribes, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:1-35</reference>. That the Euphrates north, Mediterranean west, the Nile and Red Sea south, are to be the future boundaries of the holy land, which will include Syria and Arabia, is favored by <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">Ge 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.31">Ex 23:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.24">De 11:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Jos 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">1Ki 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.26">2Ch 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Is 27:12</reference>; all which was partially realized in Solomon's reign, shall be antitypically so hereafter. The theory, if true, will clear away many difficulties in the way of the literal interpretation of this chapter and <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:1-35</reference>. <div eID="gen24913" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 5. ye shall flee to the valley-- rather "through the valley," as in 2Sa 2:29 . The valley made by the cleaving asunder of the Mount of Olives ( Zec 14:4 ) is designed to be their way of escape, not their place of refuge [Maurer]. Jerome is on the side of English Version. If it be translated so, it will mean, Ye shall flee "to" the valley, not to hide there, but as the passage through which an escape may be effected. The same divinely sent earthquake which swallows up the foe, opens out a way of escape to God's people. The earthquake in Uzziah's days is mentioned ( Am 1:1 ) as a recognized epoch in Jewish history. Compare also Is 6:1 : perhaps the same year that Jehovah held His heavenly court and gave commission to Isaiah for the Jews, an earthquake in the physical world, as often happens ( Mt 24:7 ), marked momentous movements in the unseen spiritual world. of the mountains-- rather, "of My mountains," namely, Zion and Moriah, peculiarly sacred to Jehovah [Moore]. Or, the mountains formed by My cleaving Olivet into two [Maurer]. Azal-- the name of a place near a gate east of the city. The Hebrew means "adjoining" [Henderson]. Others give the meaning, "departed," "ceased." The valley reaches up to the city gates, so as to enable the fleeing citizens to betake themselves immediately to it on leaving the city. Lord my God ... with thee-- The mention of the "Lord my God" leads the prophet to pass suddenly to a direct address to Jehovah. It is as if "lifting up his head" ( Lu 21:28 ), he suddenly sees in vision the Lord coming, and joyfully exclaims, "All the saints with Thee!" So Is 25:9 . saints-- holy angels escorting the returning King ( Mt 24:30 , 31 ; Jude 14); and redeemed men ( 1Co 15:23 ; 1Th 3:13 ; 4:14 ). Compare the similar mention of the "saints" and "angels" at His coming on Sinai ( De 32:2 , 3 ; Ac 7:53 ; Ga 3:19 ; He 2:2 ). Phillips thinks Azal is Ascalon on the Mediterranean. An earthquake beneath Messiah's tread will divide Syria, making from Jerusalem to Azal a valley which will admit the ocean waters from the west to the Dead Sea. The waters will rush down the valley of Arabah, the old bed of the Jordan, clear away the sand-drift of four thousand years, and cause the commerce of Petra and Tyre to center in the holy city. The Dead Sea rising above its shores will overflow by the valley of Edom, completing the straits of Azal into the Red Sea. Thus will be formed the great pool of Jerusalem (compare Zec 14:8 ; Eze 47:1 , &c.; Joe 3:18 ). Euphrates will be the north boundary, and the Red Sea the south. Twenty-five miles north and twenty-five miles south of Jerusalem will form one side of the fifty miles square of the Lord's Holy Oblation ( Eze 48:1-35 ). There are seven spaces of fifty miles each from Jerusalem northward to the Euphrates, and five spaces of fifty miles each southward to the Red Sea. Thus there are thirteen equal distances on the breadth of the future promised land, one for the oblation and twelve for the tribes, according to Eze 48:1-35 . That the Euphrates north, Mediterranean west, the Nile and Red Sea south, are to be the future boundaries of the holy land, which will include Syria and Arabia, is favored by Ge 15:8 ; Ex 23:31 ; De 11:24 ; Jos 1:4 ; 1Ki 4:21 ; 2Ch 9:26 ; Is 27:12 ; all which was partially realized in Solomon's reign, shall be antitypically so hereafter. The theory, if true, will clear away many difficulties in the way of the literal interpretation of this chapter and Eze 48:1-35 .

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13197"/><div sID="gen24914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13197"/><hi type="bold">6. light ... not ... clear ... dark--</hi>Jerome, Chaldee, Syriac, and Septuagint translate, "There shall not be light, but cold and ice"; that is, a day full of horror (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference>). But the Hebrew for "clear" does not mean "cold," but "precious," "splendid" (compare <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>). Calvin translates, "The light shall not be clear, but dark" (literally, "condensation," that is, thick mist); like a dark day in which you can hardly distinguish between day and night. English Version accords with <reference osisRef="Zech.14.7">Zec 14:7</reference>: "There shall not be altogether light nor altogether darkness," but an intermediate condition in which sorrows shall be mingled with joys. <div eID="gen24914" type="x-p"/>

Compare "one," that is, unique (<reference osisRef="Song.6.9">So 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">Jr 30:7</reference>). Not as Henderson explains, "One continuous day, without night" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.5">Re 22:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.25">21:25</reference>); the millennial period (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.3-Rev.20.7">Re 20:3-7</reference>).<div eID="gen24915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">known to ... Lord--</hi>This truth restrains man's curiosity and teaches us to wait the Lord's own time (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.36">Mt 24:36</reference>).<div eID="gen24916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not day, nor night--</hi>answering to "not ... clear nor ... dark" (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.6">Zec 14:6</reference>); not altogether daylight, yet not the darkness of night.<div eID="gen24917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at evening ... shall be light--</hi>Towards the close of this twilight-like time of calamity, "light" shall spring up (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.11">Psa 97:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">112:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Is 30:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">60:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen24918" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 7. one day-- a day altogether unique, different from all others [Maurer]. Compare "one," that is, unique ( So 6:9 ; Jr 30:7 ). Not as Henderson explains, "One continuous day, without night" ( Re 22:5 ; 21:25 ); the millennial period ( Re 20:3-7 ). known to ... entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13202"/><div sID="gen24934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13202"/><hi type="bold">11. no more utter destruction--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.31.40">Jr 31:40</reference>). Literally, "no more curse" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">Re 22:3</reference>; compare Mal 4:6), for there will be no more sin. Temporal blessings and spiritual prosperity shall go together in the millennium: long life (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.20-Isa.65.22">Is 65:20-22</reference>), peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>), honor (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.14-Isa.60.16">Is 60:14-16</reference>), righteous government (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.14">Is 54:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.18">60:18</reference>). Judgment, as usual, begins at the house of God, but then falls fatally on Antichrist, whereon the Church obtains perfect liberty. The last day will end everything evil (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Ro 8:21</reference>) [Auberlen]. <div eID="gen24934" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13207"/><div sID="gen24940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13207"/><hi type="bold">16. every one ... left--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">23</reference>). God will conquer all the foes of the Church. Some He will destroy; others He will bring into willing subjection.<div eID="gen24940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from year to year--</hi>literally, "from the sufficiency of a year in a year."<div eID="gen24941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feast of tabernacles--</hi>The other two great yearly feasts, passover and pentecost, are not specified, because, their antitypes having come, the types are done away with. But the feast of tabernacles will be commemorative of the Jews' sojourn, not merely forty years in the wilderness, but for almost two thousand years of their dispersion. So it was kept on their return from the Babylonian dispersion (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.14-Neh.8.17">Ne 8:14-17</reference>). It was the feast on which Jesus made His triumphal entry into Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.8">Mt 21:8</reference>); a pledge of His return to His capital to reign (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Le 23:34</reference>, 39, 40, 42; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">21:3</reference>). A feast of peculiar joy (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.15">Psa 118:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">Ho 12:9</reference>). The feast on which Jesus gave the invitation to the living waters of salvation ("Hosanna," save us now, was the cry, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Mt 21:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.25">Psa 118:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.26">26</reference>) (<reference osisRef="John.7.2">Joh 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.37">37</reference>). To the Gentiles, too, it will be significant of perfected salvation after past wanderings in a moral wilderness, as it originally commemorated the ingathering of the harvest. The seedtime of tears shall then have issued in the harvest of joy [Moore]. "All the nations" could not possibly in person go up to the feast, but they may do so by representatives. <div eID="gen24942" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13209"/><div sID="gen24944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13209"/><hi type="bold">18. if ... Egypt go not up--</hi>specified as Israel's ancient foe. If Egypt go not up, and so there be no rain on them (a judgment which Egypt would condemn, as depending on the Nile's overflow, not on rain), there shall be the plague ... . Because the guilty are not affected by one judgment, let them not think to escape, for God has other judgments which shall plague them. Maurer translates, "If Egypt go not up, upon them also there shall be none" (no rain). <reference osisRef="Ps.105.32">Psa 105:32</reference> mentions "rain" in Egypt. But it is not their main source of fertility. <div eID="gen24944" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13211"/><div sID="gen24946" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13211"/><hi type="bold">20. shall there be upon the bells--</hi>namely, this inscription, "Holiness to the Lord," the same as was on the miter of the high priest (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.36">Ex 28:36</reference>). This implies that all things, even the most common, shall be sacred to Jehovah, and not merely the things which under the law had peculiar sanctity attached to them. The "bells" were metal plates hanging from the necks of horses and camels as ornaments, which tinkled (as the Hebrew root means) by striking against each other. Bells attached to horses are found represented on the walls of Sennacherib's palace at Koyunjik.<div eID="gen24946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pots ... like ... bowls--</hi>the vessels used for boiling, for receiving ashes, &c., shall be as holy as the bowls used for catching the blood of the sacrificial victims (see on <reference osisRef="Zech.9.15">Zec 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.14">1Sa 2:14</reference>). The priesthood of Christ will be explained more fully both by the Mosaic types and by the New Testament in that temple of which Ezekiel speaks. Then the Song of Solomon, now obscure, will be understood, for the marriage feast of the Lamb will be celebrated in heaven (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.21">Re 19:1-21</reference>), and on earth it will be a Solomonic period, peaceful, glorious, and nuptial. There will be no king but a prince; the sabbatic period of the judges will return, but not with the Old Testament, but New Testament glory (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Is 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.1-Ezek.45.25">Eze 45:1-25</reference>) [Roos]. <div eID="gen24947" type="x-p"/>
